phonemes.desc: Aspirated rho [rʰ], the breathy initial consonant preserved in the rough breathing.
Short epsilon with acute [é], the pitch peak of the name.
Long alpha [aː], the feminine ending that gives the name its dignity.

pronunciation.approximation: 'RHAY-ah' — begin with a breathy 'r', stress the middle syllable, and draw out the final 'ah'.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Ῥέα (Rhéā), Titaness, mother of the Olympian gods

kin.label: Etymology
kin.form: Possibly related to ῥέω (rhéō), 'to flow'; etymology uncertain

kin.label: Anatolian
kin.form: Some scholars compare her to Anatolian mother goddesses; the connection is debated

pronunciation.note: Rhéā is Tier 2 because the Greek Ῥέα preserves the acute stress on the second syllable and length on the final alpha, but the stress and length fall on different syllables. She is the great mother of the Olympian generation.

domains.title: Mother of the Gods
domains.subtitle: Fertility, Mountain, Maternal Cunning
domains.lead: Rhéā is the Titaness who gave birth to the Olympian gods and saved the youngest, Zeus, from being swallowed by his father Kronos. She is the mountain mother, the fertile earth, and the cunning protector of divine succession.

cards.name: Mother of Olympians
cards.desc: By Kronos she bore Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, Poseidon, and Zeus.

cards.name: Protector of Zeus
cards.desc: She hid the infant Zeus in a Cretan cave and gave Kronos a stone in swaddling clothes.

cards.name: Mountain Goddess
cards.desc: Worshipped on Crete and in Phrygia as a mother of wild things and mountains.

cards.name: Fertility and Flow
cards.desc: Her name's possible link to 'flow' connects her to springs, milk, and abundance.

symbols.name: Swaddled stone (Omphalos)
symbols.meaning: The substitute she gave Kronos to save Zeus

symbols.name: Cretan cave
symbols.meaning: The hiding place of the infant Zeus on Mount Ida or Dikte

symbols.name: Lion
symbols.meaning: Her attendant beast in later Cybele-like iconography

symbols.name: Tympanon drum
symbols.meaning: The percussion instrument of ecstatic mountain cults associated with the Great Mother

mythology.lead: Rhéā's myth is the hinge between Titanic and Olympian rule. She endures Kronos's violence, then engineers the survival of the son who will overthrow him.

myths.title: The Swallowed Children
myths.text: Kronos, warned that one of his children would overthrow him, swallowed each infant as Rhea bore them. Rhea wept but was powerless until the birth of Zeus. Then she turned from grieving mother to strategist.

myths.title: The Ruse of the Stone
myths.text: Rhea asked her parents Gē and Ouranos for advice. They sent her to Crete, where she gave birth to Zeus in a hidden cave. She wrapped a great stone in swaddling clothes and presented it to Kronos, who swallowed it unaware. The stone was later set up at Delphi as the omphalos.

myths.title: The Kouretes
myths.text: To hide the infant Zeus's cries, Rhea's attendants the Kouretes clashed their weapons and danced. The ritual became a Cretan mystery: the birth of the god was protected by noise, movement, and collective vigilance.

lore.syncretism: Rhéā was identified with the Anatolian Great Mother Cybele and, to some extent, with the Cretan mother of Zeus. The Romans called her Ops, the goddess of abundance and the consort of Saturn. Her cult blurred into that of Gē, Demeter, and Cybele, all embodiments of the fertile earth. The lion-drawn chariot and tympanon of Cybele were sometimes transferred to Rhea in Hellenistic and Roman art.
lore.culturalLegacy: Rhéā is the mother without whom there is no Olympus. Her courage in saving Zeus made the Olympian order possible. In modern usage her name labels one of Saturn's moons and appears in fantasy and science fiction as a figure of primordial motherhood. Her myth remains a powerful story of maternal resistance against patriarchal violence.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Rhéā is the mother who learns to deceive in order to protect. She does not confront Kronos directly; she outwits him with a stone. This is not weakness but strategic love — the recognition that survival sometimes requires cunning rather than force.

Her story also holds grief. She bore children only to lose them to her husband's belly. The stone she substitutes is a monument to what was swallowed: time, memory, innocence. When it is vomited up and displayed at Delphi, it becomes the center of the world. Rhea teaches that the things hidden in darkness can become, in time, the axis of a new order.
lore.archaeology: Rhea was worshipped on Crete in caves associated with the birth of Zeus, including the Idaian and Diktaian caves. The Corybantes and Kouretes were her ecstatic attendants in Cretan and Phrygian cult. In mainland Greece she was often conflated with the Great Mother; her distinction from Cybele is not always clear in the archaeological record. The omphalos stone at Delphi was identified with the swaddled stone of Zeus.
